# The 'sustainability-data' Well-Known URI (IETF Internet-Draft)

> A uniform, out-of-band convention for web servers and digital services to publish their aggregated environmental impact, energy consumption, and carbon footprint metrics.

## Project Links
* **GitHub Repository:** https://github.com/andreibesleaga/rfc-sustainability-wellknown
* **IETF Datatracker:** https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-besleaga-sustainability-wellknown/
* **Author:** Andrei Nicolae Besleaga (https://github.com/andreibesleaga)
* **IETF Stream:** Independent Submission (individual; not a working-group product)
* **Current Draft Status:** `-07`, **in preparation and not yet posted** to the Datatracker (do not cite it as posted or published). It withdraws the companion `/.well-known/sustainability-data.jws` resource and its detached signature entirely — no legacy support, no redirect, no fallback — replacing it with an OPTIONAL `signed` member embedded in each declaration object; removes the `version` member, leaving exactly seven mandatory members; closes the top-level member set and moves private extensions into an OPTIONAL `extensions` object keyed by absolute URI (RFC 3986) instead of reverse-domain top-level names; adds an OPTIONAL `upstream` member linking to the declarations a subject's figures derive from; replaces the old free/unauthenticated-methodology conformance floor with a simpler "at least one numeric metric, `disclosure-uri`, or `verifiable-attestation-uri`" rule; gives Extended Query Parameters an ABNF grammar and a numbered processing procedure with defined `400`/`404` cases; drops the server-side 366-object cap in favor of a consumer-side byte/object bound; and drops the `X-Content-Type-Options` recommendation from the specification text.
* **`-06`** (posted 2026-09-10, under ISE review): the **latest posted** revision. It responds to the ISE's second round (security designed in from the start) and to the first commissioned review: it requests registration of the `application/sustainability-data+json` media type in the standards tree and requires it, makes HTTPS a MUST, adds an OPTIONAL detached-JWS signature mechanism at a companion well-known resource, restructures the Security Considerations around a threat-model table, adds a "Roles and Processing Model" section and a "Partial Knowledge and Incremental Adoption" section, and fixes the `version` label as a single defined value — all with no wire-format change from `-05`. (`-07`, above, supersedes the detached-JWS, `version`, and `nosniff` points of this paragraph; this remains an accurate record of what `-06` shipped.)
* **`-05`** (posted 2026-07-28): responded to the ISE's initial review of `-04` — removing the carbon.txt-path reference from `disclosure-uri` (now format- and location-agnostic), adding an Internationalization Considerations section, and recognizing the calendar year as the common Basic-service reporting cycle — with no wire-format change.
* **`-04`** (also posted): renamed the requested well-known URI suffix from `sustainability` to `sustainability-data` (per ISE feedback on RFC 8615's precision expectations, resolving the IANA well-known-URI naming feedback), added the optional `target-type` member, placed the `version` value space under change control, and defined the reverse-domain extension-member naming rule. `-03` (posted 2026-07-23) is an earlier posted revision.

## Context and Purpose
The digital economy consumes a significant percentage of global electricity. Regulatory frameworks (like the EU CSRD) and industry standards (like GSF SCI, W3C Web Sustainability Guidelines) increasingly require organizations to disclose their digital environmental impact. 

An earlier per-request HTTP-header approach to carbon transparency was explored first — filed as `draft-besleaga-green-sustainability-header-00` (now expired) — and set aside in favor of this well-known URI's out-of-band design, which avoids the per-request "rebound effect" (metadata increasing the footprint it reports). This project proposes an alternative: leveraging RFC 8615 to define a discoverable `/.well-known/sustainability-data` URI for asynchronous, out-of-band reporting. This allows workflows where environmental impact is a primary constraint alongside cost and performance.

**Applicability is broader than conventional websites.** RFC 8615 well-known URIs are scoped to an HTTP(S) *origin* (scheme+host+port), not to "a website" — any HTTP-speaking device or service can serve one. That includes IoT/embedded devices (constrained devices already use the analogous convention, CoAP's `/.well-known/core`, registered by RFC 6690) and Web3/blockchain infrastructure (an RPC gateway or validator dashboard is an ordinary HTTP origin). The data model is entity-level, not hosting-level: `provider` names the operating entity, and the reference implementation's enterprise adapters (Salesforce NZC, Microsoft Sustainability Manager, Watershed) are written to populate documents from organization-level reporting platforms rather than server telemetry; they run in the gateway against recorded responses, none has been exercised against a live tenant, and the Microsoft adapter targets a preview API retired 2025-05-30 — so the same endpoint can carry a regulator-mandated organizational disclosure (e.g. EU CSRD, or the EU MiCA consensus-mechanism energy/carbon disclosure already required of crypto-asset issuers), not only a website's own hosting footprint.

## Repository Structure & Resources
In addition to tracking the evolution of the draft through standard IETF versions (the former `draft-besleaga-green-sustainability-wellknown-00`…`-05` series, continued as `draft-besleaga-sustainability-wellknown-00`…`-06`, of which `-06` is the latest posted revision and `-07` is in preparation, unposted), the GitHub repository acts as an extended resource hub for implementers. It includes:
* **Draft Sources (`internet-drafts/`):** The core `.md` (Markdown) files which act as the source documents compiled into the final IETF `.xml`/`.txt` formats using the kramdown-rfc + xml2rfc toolchains, plus a `CHANGELOG.md` and a supplementary W3C Verifiable Credential structure.
* **Schemas & Validators (`schemas-validators/`):** Formal machine-readable definitions of the JSON data model — JSON Type Definition (JTD, RFC 8927) and Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL, RFC 8610) — with Python (JTD) and Ruby (CDDL) validators and a `validate-all.sh` runner.
* **Examples (`example-responses/`):** 22 sample JSON responses demonstrating Basic, Extended, Target-Specific, and annual-reporting scenarios — including origin/organization/service/product/device/tenant/data-source `target-type` examples, the `-07` upstream pair (a downstream organization and the tenant-scoped declaration it names), and a minimum-conformance example, and a comprehensive data-centre-operator report carrying every optional member that fits an organization plus six `https`-keyed extensions (facility ISO/IEC 30134 KPIs, water, waste, hardware circularity, direct emissions, renewable procurement). All pass both validators.
* **Reference Implementation (`publisher/`):** A reference TypeScript publisher that serves a conformant `/.well-known/sustainability-data` from pluggable source adapters (static/computed, Kepler/Prometheus, Climatiq, Green Web Foundation CO2.js [bytes→carbon], the Green Web Foundation carbon.txt hosted API, Salesforce Net Zero Cloud, Microsoft Sustainability Manager, Watershed). It normalizes units, validates every payload against the JTD/CDDL schemas before serving, and ships as Express/Fastify middleware and a standalone server. It can also serve a bidirectional `carbon.txt` (emit/parse/discover helper) that points back to the metrics document. Includes example security middleware (`example-scripts/`) and web-server configs (`server-configurations/`). Published on npm as **`sustainability-wellknown-publisher`** (registry 0.1.0 implements the historical -02/"1.1" model; 0.4.0 through 0.6.7 implement the "2.0" model, and **0.7.1 is the current release** (0.7.0 plus one change: an unmatched `target` gets the same 404 body as a no-data period), implementing `-07`'s payload changes — the embedded `signed` member replacing the detached JWS, the closed member set, `extensions`, and `upstream` — while `0.6.0` had added the `-06` media type and HTTPS, and `0.6.5` had added the (now withdrawn) detached-JWS signature, the vc+jwt attestation, and the consumer's --verify).
* **Reference Client (`consumer/`):** A TypeScript reference *client* for `/.well-known/sustainability-data`, complementing the publisher's reference *producer*. It fetches a document from any origin, defensively validates it (JTD schema plus the draft's cross-entry array rules), transforms it (CSV, NDJSON, a flattened one-row-per-metric shape, trend aggregation), and doubles as a standalone conformance checker (its `sustainability-fetch --strict` CLI). It ships a zero-dependency one-call `fetchSustainability` function and a richer ETag-caching `SustainabilityClient` class, and is interop-tested in-process against a real `Publisher` — demonstrating the full produce→fetch→validate→transform lifecycle across two independent implementations. Published on npm as **`sustainability-wellknown-consumer`** (same versioning note as the publisher).
* **Supporting Docs:** `ADOPTION.md` (the case for RFC/IANA adoption) and `sfc-compliance/` — `PROFILE.md`, the normative SFC profile of this well-known URI (four criteria, network and operator declaration levels, three extension names under `https://andreibesleaga.com/sfc/extensions/`, and what a conformance statement may claim), two reference declarations in `examples/`, the `sfc-check.mjs` checker built on the published consumer, and the older non-normative note `SFC.md` mapping this draft's members onto the author's own Sustainability-First Consensus framework.

## Key Technical Specifications

### The Endpoint
* **Path:** `/.well-known/sustainability-data`
* **Method:** HTTP GET (and HEAD; other methods get `405` with `Allow: GET, HEAD`)
* **Protocol:** HTTPS (MUST)
* **Response:** `200 OK` with `application/sustainability-data+json` payload (MUST NOT use another media type; a consumer MUST process it and MAY also process `application/json`, under which documents published before the registration are found, and SHOULD send `Accept: application/sustainability-data+json, application/json;q=0.9`), or `404 Not Found` if no metadata exists. Successful responses SHOULD follow I-JSON (RFC 7493) and SHOULD carry `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (CORS, for browser-based clients). (`-07` drops the `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` recommendation from the specification; implementations may still send it operationally.)

### Query Parameters
Servers MUST support a "Basic" service level: a `GET` with no query parameters answered `200 OK` with the declaration, covering whatever subject its `target` names over whatever period its `reporting-period` names. (`-07` drops the `-06`-era rules that the Basic response be a single object covering the most recently completed period and the full declared subject; what remains is that figures covering part of a declared subject MUST NOT be presented as the whole. A full calendar year, served as a plain static file, is still the common case.) Servers MAY support "Extended" capabilities to filter data. `-07` gives the query string a formal ABNF grammar (RFC 5234) and a numbered processing procedure:
* `target`: Specific resource path prefix (e.g., `?target=/api/v1`); a server scoping a response to it echoes the matched prefix in the mandatory `target` member, and honors only a set of prefixes it MUST publish in the document its `methodology-uri` identifies — a `target` outside that set yields the same `404 Not Found` the server returns when it holds no data, which it SHOULD make indistinguishable in body and timing.
* `period`: Timeframe as a calendar-date precision form — Year `YYYY`, Month `YYYY-MM`, or Day `YYYY-MM-DD` (only the last is an RFC 3339 `full-date`); interpreted in UTC. A malformed or non-real `period` yields `400 Bad Request`. Without a finer `granularity`, a `period` request yields a single object (or 404 per the no-data rule), never an array.
* `granularity`: Time slices within a period (`monthly`, `daily`); an unrecognized or too-coarse value is ignored. When finer than the period, returns an array of objects sorted ascending. `-07` removes the server-side 366-object cap; a conforming response is bounded only by the calendar, and a consumer MUST bound the bytes and objects it accepts instead of relying on any server-side limit.
* A duplicated query-parameter name yields `400 Bad Request`.

**Key distinction:** the *origin* is where the document is published; the `target` member is what the metrics are about — they coincide for origin-wide reports (the origin's host), but `target` may equally name an organization, a path, a cloud tenant, a device, or a data source.

### Data Model
As of `-07` the response schema defines 7 mandatory + 19 optional members (26 total); the `version` member of `-04`–`-06` (fixed at `"2.0"`) is removed and the media type alone identifies the format:
* **Mandatory Fields (7):**
  * `updated`: RFC 3339 timestamp of last update.
  * `capabilities`: "basic" or "extended" — describes **query-parameter support only** (a "basic" document MAY carry any optional members).
  * `provider`: Information about the publisher.
  * `measurement-method`: e.g., `hardware-metered`, `hardware-estimated`, `cloud-billing`, `third-party-modeled`.
  * `methodology-uri`: Link to the full calculation methodology.
  * `reporting-period`: The timeframe covered.
  * `target`: Opaque identifier of the reporting subject — a protocol element compared octet-for-octet and never translated — origin host (RECOMMENDED for origin-wide reports), path prefix, organizational entity, cloud tenant, or software data source; echoes the matched prefix when the response is `target` query-scoped.
* **Optional Fields (19):** `target-type` (an enumerated hint classifying the reporting subject named by `target`: `origin`, `path`, `organization`, `service`, `product`, `device`, `tenant`, `data-source`; unrecognized values are tolerated — the client interprets `target` as if the member were absent; in arrays the member is all-or-none: every entry carries the same value or none carries it), `energy-consumption` (non-negative) & `energy-unit` (Wh, kWh, MWh, GWh; default `kWh` when absent), `carbon-footprint` (gross, non-negative) & `carbon-unit` (gCO2e, kgCO2e, mtCO2e; default `gCO2e` when absent, also parameterizing scopes), `carbon-accounting` (location/market-based), `scope-1`, `scope-2`, `scope-3` emissions (MAY be negative — removals/net accounting), `sci-score` (non-negative; requires `functional-unit`), `functional-unit`, `carbon-intensity-gCO2e-per-kWh`, `estimated-annual-emissions-kgCO2e`, `renewable-energy` percentage (0–100 inclusive), `verifiable-attestation-uri` (at most one per declaration; a subject with more than one attestation links an index of them from `disclosure-uri`), `disclosure-uri` (a format- and location-agnostic URI to a machine-readable sustainability disclosure index; the Green Web Foundation's carbon.txt convention is one such form among others, cited as complementary work), `upstream` (array of `{ declaration: <absolute https URI of another declaration>, role?: hosting/cloud/cdn/network/electricity }` — declarations a subject's figures derive from; a consumer MAY walk the chain to depth 3, no revisits, comparing same-period figures as evidence, never proof), `extensions` (object keyed by absolute URI, RFC 3986 — an `https` URI under the definer's control, which SHOULD identify human-readable documentation of the extension, or `urn:uuid:` plus a lowercase hyphenated UUID, RFC 9562, for a definer without a domain; a key is an identifier compared as a string, never dereferenced, and there is no registry; a consumer that does not implement a key's definition ignores its value and never dereferences or executes anything within it), and `signed` (the embedded JWS — see Signing below).
* **Minimum reporting rule:** a declaration object MUST carry at least one numeric metric member, or `disclosure-uri`, or `verifiable-attestation-uri`; an object with none of the three is not conformant. (The `-06` condition requiring the `methodology-uri` resource itself to be free and unauthenticated when no metric was present is removed in `-07`.)
* **Closed top-level member set:** a publisher MUST NOT add other top-level members; a consumer ignores one it does not recognize. Private extension data goes in `extensions` (above), not as an additional top-level member.
* **Omitted metrics & legacy compatibility:** omission is the only "not reported" mechanism — no in-band sentinel exists. Historical `1.x` documents used a negative sentinel and an optional `target-path` member. The packages (not the specification) additionally tolerate historical documents: they apply field-driven compatibility/tolerance rules (a negative value in a non-negative member = not reported; a wrong-JSON-type value, including `null`, = not reported/absent; an `sci-score` without `functional-unit` = absent; a missing `target` = origin-wide report; a legacy document carrying `target-path` = metrics attributed to that declared subject, not the origin).
* **Readiness (by design):** web-ready (plain HTTPS GET, standard caching/conditional requests), API/M2M-ready (stable JSON + formal CDDL/JTD schemas + deterministic semantics), human-readable (self-describing member names + mandatory methodology link), and AI/agent-ready (fixed discoverable location, schema-validatable, no content negotiation needed).

### Signing (the `signed` member, since `-07`)
Each declaration object MAY carry an OPTIONAL `signed` member: a JWS Compact Serialization whose payload is that same object minus `signed`, with protected header `alg` (EdDSA or ES256; `none` and MACs are rejected), `cty: "sustainability-data+json"`, and the key as `jwk`/`x5c`/`kid`. A consumer verifies it only when present — absence means unsigned, never an error. Precedence depends on how far the key is trusted: where it was obtained out of band, pinned from an earlier retrieval, or chained through `x5c` to a trusted anchor, the verified payload's values are the ones used; in every other case the key is trusted no further than the declaration carrying it and the members the origin served remain the ones used (pinning gives continuity of authorship, not identity). Either way a mismatch is reported as "modified after signing", not a verification failure. `-07` withdraws the `-06`-era companion resource `/.well-known/sustainability-data.jws` and its detached signature entirely: there is no legacy support, no redirect, no fallback.

## Important Considerations
* **Caching & DoS:** Heavy caching (e.g., `Cache-Control: max-age=86400`) and rate-limiting are strongly recommended because dynamic aggregation queries can be resource-intensive. `ETag` and `Last-Modified` headers are RECOMMENDED.
* **Privacy & Traffic Analysis:** Finer-than-24-hour granularity is discouraged to prevent correlating energy spikes with real-time user actions.
* **Hardware Fingerprinting:** An optional ~1% multiplicative (sign-preserving) "fuzzing" of metrics helps obscure specific backend hardware architectures with limited impact on aggregate accuracy; if applied, it is applied once at generation time, deterministically per reporting period, and consistently across related fields — non-negative members stay non-negative and negative scope values keep their sign.
* **Greenwashing Mitigation:** The specification does not mandate verification but provides schema surfaces (like `verifiable-attestation-uri`) to link to cryptographically signed W3C Verifiable Credentials or third-party attestations.
* **Internationalization (added in the posted `-05` revision):** Member names, enumerated values, dates, URIs, `target`, `functional-unit`, the `role` tokens, the `extensions` URI keys, `signed`, and the RECOMMENDED `measurement-method` tokens are protocol elements — compared octet-for-octet and never localized; free-text members (`provider`, a non-RECOMMENDED `measurement-method` description, human-readable values inside `extensions`) carry language via `Content-Language`, optionally negotiated with `Accept-Language` (with `Vary`).

## Extensibility & Versioning
* **The `version` member is removed as of `-07`.** `-04` through `-06` carried it as an informational label, fixed by `-06` at the single value `"2.0"`; the media type alone now identifies the format, and there is no version member at all to be informational about.
* **The top-level member set is closed.** A publisher MUST NOT add other top-level members; a consumer ignores one it does not recognize, with a warning. Forward compatibility for the *defined* member set still rests on the must-ignore rule for members a future revision of the specification adds.
* **Private extensions live in the OPTIONAL `extensions` object, keyed by an absolute URI** (RFC 3986 absolute-URI: ASCII, scheme in lowercase, no fragment), replacing the `-04`–`-06` reverse-domain-name convention (`com.example.pue`) and the "undotted names reserved for the specification" rule. Two forms are used in practice: an `https` URI under the definer's control when the name was minted, which SHOULD identify human-readable documentation of the extension, and `urn:uuid:` followed by the lowercase hyphenated text form of a UUID (RFC 9562, Section 4) for a definer that has no domain or wants a name independent of one — the Nil and Max UUIDs MUST NOT be used. The name identifies the party that defines its value's members; the definer chooses it once and publishes the definition wherever it chooses. Keys are compared as strings, octet for octet, and are never dereferenced — so a later change of domain ownership does not change what an existing document means — and no registry is defined. The model is RFC 7519's Collision-Resistant Name and RFC 8288's extension relation types. A publisher's methodology document SHOULD list the extension names it uses with their definitions. A consumer that does not implement a name's definition MUST ignore that value and MUST NOT dereference or execute anything within it.
* New top-level members can still only be introduced by a future revision of this specification, under the must-ignore rule; private, un-standardized data always goes inside `extensions`, never as a new top-level name.
